VideoTitle: Laravel From Scratch [Part 5] - Models & Database Migrations
CommentText:
I'm following these tutorials with PHP 7.4.9 / Laravel 8 and MAMP 6.0.1 and all good so far - until I attempted to do the  php artisan migrate  step in this video. And then, I got this this error :

SQLSTATE[HY000] [1045] Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost' (using password: NO) (SQL: select * from information_schema.tables where table_schema = lsapp and table_name = migrations and table_type = 'BASE TABLE') 

I resolved it thanks to a stack overflow post that advised that you need to add this to your .env file : 

DB_SOCKET=/Applications/MAMP/tmp/mysql/mysql.sock 

...so Laravel knows where to find mysql. Also, NB if you're using MAMP, you need to amend the DB_HOST and DB_PORT settings to match MAMP. 

To summarise, here's what the relevant bit of my .env file looks like which allows the  php artisan migrate  task to run correctly : 

DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=8889
DB_DATABASE=lsapp
DB_USERNAME=root
DB_PASSWORD=root
DB_SOCKET=/Applications/MAMP/tmp/mysql/mysql.sock

class Solution:
    def characterReplacement(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        l=0
        r=0
        maxi=0
        ans=0
        temp=0
        n=len(s)
        hm={}
        while(r<n):
            
            if s[r] not in hm:
                hm[s[r]]=1
            else:
                hm[s[r]]+=1
            #to find most frequent character
            maxi=max(maxi,hm[s[r]])
            t=r-l+1

            if abs(t-maxi)>k:
                #shrinking the window and decreasing most frequent character
                hm[s[l]]-=1
                l+=1
        
            ans=max(ans,r-l+1)

            r+=1
        return ans

Thank you for the excellent video. As a programmer with 50 years of experience, I must say that we have lost touch with algorithms in the sense I discuss in my articles on Medium: "Bagels and Muffins of Programming or How Easy It Is to Convert a Bagel into a Black Hole"

Thinking algorithmically and living in an algorithm-centric world of software engineering, creating muffin-like programs, is now the domain of a few solitary individuals. Today's programming world increasingly focuses on a code-centric approach, where algorithms are not seen as separate entities. This shift has led to significant changes in how we develop and maintain software.

There was a time when algorithms were at the heart of any program, providing a clear and understandable structure for development. They helped us build logical and efficient solutions. However, with the rise of high-level programming languages and frameworks, the emphasis shifted to quickly writing code and implementing new features, often at the expense of structured algorithmic thinking.

Nowadays, we often encounter bagel-like programs where the code exists separately from the algorithm, creating internal inconsistencies and maintenance difficulties. In such conditions, achieving stability and reliability in software becomes challenging.

Returning to an algorithm-centric approach and creating muffin-like programs, where the algorithm and code are integrated, can significantly improve the quality of software. This will not only simplify testing and maintenance but also allow for more flexible and resilient systems.

I hope more developers will begin to recognize the importance of algorithms and move towards a more structured and meaningful approach to programming. Only in this way can we create software that is reliable, understandable, and easy to maintain.

VideoTitle: The Programming Language Guide
CommentText:
I think you're missing the distinction between managed languages and interpreted languages. Managed languages such as Java and C# are compiled into intermediate bytecode and then execute on a virtual machine. This means they're perfectly portable to any system that has a VM for that language and supports the required features of the individual program (keyboard vs touchscreen, etc).

Interpreted/scripting languages are executed from uncompiled source in real time. These days they mostly use just-in-time (JIT) compilation on a line-by-line basis, but they intentionally hold on to the line-by-line execution model because it means that scripts can be edited while their program is running. This is incredibly convenient for things like coding NPC behavior in a video game, since you can tweak and test without needing to stop, recompile, and restart. You can literally just change the script in a text editor, then alt+tab back to the game and trigger the new behavior to see how it works out.

The downside is performance, of course, since each new line has to be interpreted as it's encountered, and there's no opportunity for whole-program optimization by the interpreter, whereas compiled or managed languages can do that, since all the code is known prior to runtime.

You mentioned utilizing a 'third method' for installing create-nuxt-app via NodeJS, but you were actually using NPM, which is indeed a part of NodeJS, along with NPX. By using NPM to run create-nuxt-app, you're essentially running the locally stored version of create-nuxt-app from when it was installed globally. NPX functions similarly to NPM -g, but it always fetches the latest version and runs it once. If you have a fast internet connection, NPX is generally preferable. If your internet isn't as fast, NPM might be a better option, but you'll be using an older version.

VideoTitle: How I Failed the Google Coding Interview (and lessons I learned)
CommentText:
I've interviewed many many candidates on coding questions. So this is a bit of the perspective from the other side. I think you probably failed most on the first 2 coding interviews. Also, AFAIK, it would not have taken 3 weeks to get the rejection if you were not close to getting an offer. Two general comments:

The worst thing is when an overly prepared candidate (a "competitive coder" type) is given a relatively easy or familiar question, and then just jumps into it without communicating much. Whether they take a wrong turn, or not, doesn't really matter. The most valuable thing is to get an opportunity to see how a candidate works through a problem they don't know already or isn't immediately obvious to them, it's really not about arriving at the solution.

The best thing to remember: The destination is already known to the interviewer, the journey is the interesting bit.

Bonus tip: If you get a question in an interview that you already know (from practice, or whatever), I would highly recommend that you just tell the interviewer right away. If you just bust out the solution quickly, he will be annoyed at the waste of time, because he will have to ask another question and with less time. If you try to pretend you don't know the question, he will see through that, believe me, programmers make terrible actors, and he will be even more annoyed. Most interviewers have many alternative questions ready to go.

And about the nodding and letting you go astray. That's typical, even expected of any decent interviewer, I would say. Doing an interview is a bit like walking a dog, you gotta let the candidate wander around a bit on their own, and reel them in at times, but you can't just hold them on a tight leash the whole time, because then you don't learn anything about them. Very often, candidates will explain what they intend to do to solve the problem, and you know it's wrong, but you nod along and let them do it (unless they've misunderstood the problem), that's just cutting them some slack to see what happens. For interviewers, this is really hard to do, because you constantly have to repress your natural instinct to be helpful and cooperative, which is what you do all the time when you're actually working. Things like nods, smiles, and timid remarks like "mmh, interesting" or "okay", are not positive signals that you're on the right path (or wrong path, for that matter), they're just polite, repressed gestures to stay friendly and passive. So, don't get too confident, but instead understand that at that moment you're entirely on your own (either shining, or screwing up). The same goes for general back-and-forth, the interviewer might probe a little bit with questions and stuff, but you will notice that they generally don't actively add anything new, just helping you think on your own or have someone to bounce ideas, like playing tennis with a brick wall. But again, it's mostly about letting you make it or break it on your own.

So here's another thing to remember: The interviewer is not trying to help you, but trying his best NOT to help you.


Obvious corollary: If the interviewer actually gives you a really helpful tip, it's probably because you're falling behind on time. A good interviewer will drop the tip during the general back-and-forth so you don't notice that the idea came from him. But if he has to interrupt you entirely to give you an obvious tip, you're probably really far off (and also, that you're not doing well on communication either, because it's probably not his first attempt at giving you that tip).

CommentText:
Looking at it for me this was an extremely complicated way to describe Fibonacci sequence. Here how I think about it (it is pretty much the same, just a different perspective, might be easier for some people to understand it.

Thinking backwards what is the last "move" we did. We either Jumped 1 step or we jumped two steps. This means that if f(n) is the function that calculates how many steps it takes to get to the n-th step f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2). Then if you continue the logic you can see how this is the same as your decision tree diagram: f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) = (f(n-2) + f(n-3)) + f(n-2) and so on.
We can easily recognize this is Fibonacci sequence, we can even see it with some examples: To get to 1 step (f(1)) you only have 1 way. 2 steps (f(2)) - 2 ways (2 or 1+1) Then to get to three f(3) we just sum the previous two f(3)= f(2)+f(1) = 2+1 = 3,
f(4)=f(3)+f(2) = 3+2=5, f(5)=f(4)+f(3)=5+3=8 and so on.
 Then depending on how we want to solve it programmatically we can choose an approach.

However, some problems get more vaguely explained, with less detail and more complexity as you progress, making it tough to find a solution. By the time you see the solution, you realize you likely wouldn't have thought of something even remotely close to it. So, setting a time limit, looking at the solution, and trying to grasp it is probably good advice.

VideoTitle: Coding Challenge 162: Self-Avoiding Walk
CommentText: I think one of the best ways to make a perfectly space filling self avoiding walk faster would be to use an idea from space filling curves and use smaller chunks of area, where you can have a set start and end location (in the first chunk this can be randomly selected), find the small space filling walk then go to the next chunk and use the end location's mirror as the start location.  In the bigger scheme you can have an order of magnitude smaller than the walk you're trying to work out to find out the perfect space filling position for those chunk's end locations to be in.  It would be much more restrictive of a walk but still give a similar end result in a much smaller amount of time, just with less availability for giant lengths of single direction movement, which in some cases would be more desirable.  I'd imagine you could also work out the math so that the shape of the smaller chunks are variable to add more variation to the walk if desired.

CommentText: Your event binding, (onDeleteTask)="deleteTask(task)", is not using the task from the event data. The task is being derived from the ngFor directive. To invoke deleteTask() with the actual data from onDeleteTask, you must use deleteTask($event) upon event firing. $event is the Angular convention representing the object passed to the emit function of EventEmitter(i.e. this.onDeleteTask.emit(task)). VideoTitle: Git MERGE vs REBASE
CommentText:
I'm a total Git noob, but I think it's generally a good practice to avoid rebasing if at all possible.  Rewriting history is a useful but extremely dangerous capability.  I personally think it's never worth it to rewrite history just to clean up the history.  I'd rather have a couple extra commits and not risk losing my work or the work of my colleagues.  

Rewriting history on your own feature branch where you are the only person looking at that branch is one thing (I still try to avoid rewriting history there if I don't have to), but working with a team of people means you should almost never be rewriting history.  If you are rewriting history, you'd better have a good reason to do so.  And you'd better know exactly what you're doing.

The small company that I work for almost lost 6 months of work because one particularly stupid developer decided to force-push when he definitely should not have.  He rewrote the history in such a way that the last 6 months of several developers work would have been lost.  Fortunately, we were lucky enough to have someone who still had the correct history locally and we used his history to correct the f*cked up history.  But it took the better part of a day to fix properly, and the dumbass who force pushed lost 2 weeks of his own work.  The consequences of using Git incorrectly are not small.  It's always necessary to know exactly what you're doing, or find someone who does.  Don't just try to fix a problem by guessing.

VideoTitle: JavaScript this Keyword
CommentText:
So from my understanding: 

NOTE: 
A *method* is a function within an object.
A *callback function* is a function passed as an argument/parameter within another function.
==============================================================================
1. The *'this'* keyword *refers to the global object* (window) when using 'this' *within* a *function*
Ex. function Hello() {
     console.log(this)     <- 'this' will *refer to global (window) object*
}

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
However,

2. When using the *'this'* keyword within a *method* (function within an object), 'this' *refers to the object* (that the method is within)
Ex. const obj = {
     function Hello() {
          console.log(this)     <- 'this' will *refer to the object* , 'obj' as the function Hello() is within the object called 'obj'
     }
}


-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Lastly,

3. When using 'this' keyword within a *callback function* , 'this' *refers to the global object (window)* again


-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Solution, 

If the callback function is within an object, then:

4. You can _insert another argument/parameter_ , 'this' - which will make the 'this' keyword (within the callback function) *refer to the object* instead. 
This is because the 'this' keyword within the method already refers to the object containing the method.
Ex. const obj = {
     names: ['Kobe', 'Lowry', 'Fred' ]

     function Hello() {                                                     <- the 'this' in "this.names.forEach..." will *refer to the object* , 'obj'   
         *this* .names.forEach(function(names)) {     <- callback function SO,
               console.log( *this* , names)                        <- 'this' will refer to the *global object (window)*
          }, *this* )                                                               <- add 'this' keyword as another argument/parameter to the callback function, NOW 
                                                                                         'this' - within the console.log() - *will refer to the object* , 'obj' instead.
     }
}

So, in the above example, if you were to remove the additional parameter - 'this' - from the callback function... point #3 would be true

VideoTitle: Dad Gives Financial Advice How to Pay Off Mortgage Faster
CommentText:
I just bought a house.

Paying it off early could be a terrible financial decision depending on your circumstances. My 400k house will cost me roughly 800k dollars over the life of the 30 year mortgage. 

The total amount of the debt is almost irrelevant unless your plan is to pay it in cash. What really matters is the interest rate. I got a 4.5% interest rate, it does not make sense to pay more than the minimum as I will get better returns from the broad market if I invest that money, returning me well over the 400k I'll end up paying in interest on the mortgage over that 30 year period.

Some people don't want to have any debt at all, but sometimes the rates are in your favor and debt is good for you. But if you are going to pay it off early, make sure you're actually paying towards the principal and make sure your contract doesn't have any kind of early pay off fees.

Ok, I have just done a quick read on both Vue and Angular documentation, esp on component. The 1st impression, creating component in Vue is easy; the syntax is quite similar to ones which I found in javascript libs for numerous purposes such as charting with Chart.js, etc.
Whereas in Angular, the syntax is basically the same as in Vue; there is always a property named template which is a part of the process called data binding. I know, Vue creator adopted good things in Angular when he created Vue.
Learning Angular will obviously take longer time, as it requires prior skill in typescript; although once typescript is conquered, the learning process may get easier. I put aside new concepts in both frameworks, because it is a matter of effort and time to grasp. 

Both frameworks actually are interesting to me now, esp when I want to code in a new different paradigm or way of thinking than React that I currently use. It will become like "Thinking in Angular/Vue" just like "Thinking in React".

Now, the question is : can we use Vue in large app/project such as finance apps, human capital management ?

VideoTitle: Python or JavaScript - Which One Should YOU Learn?
CommentText:
When choosing a programming language to learn for a career path or career change, the first thing you should do is ask yourself: do I have the necessary background for a job that requires technical skills (which can be self-taught) and professional experience in a similar context, or can I also apply for jobs with academic requirements? There's no use in starting to learn Python to become a Data Scientist if you don't have a Master's degree, preferably in fields such as Computer Science, Statistics, Math, etc. In such cases, your academic qualifications will determine if you'll get the job or not. Knowing Python and/or being willing to learn languages/scripts that are necessary for the job would be a big plus, but not the main requirement: companies know/assume that someone with a Ph.D. or Master's degree will be able to pick up the necessary parts of the required programming language in a reasonable amount of time and at a sufficient level. On the other hand, it won't be easy or might even be close to impossible for a self-taught or bootcamp programmer to achieve the academic level of knowledge and mindset without going to college/university.

In short: if you are academically qualified, you can pick any programming language based on your interest (front-end, data science, machine learning, software engineering, etc.). If you have only self-taught and self-acquired technical skills, then pick a programming language for positions that ask for professional experience and specific technical skills, without necessarily requiring an academic degree.

Keep in mind that no matter what language you pickâespecially as a beginnerâdon't mix but specialize in one. Absolutely, there are companies looking for candidates specialized in that language. However, there are none looking for someone who has only scratched the surface of three languages but can't do anything worthwhile in any of them.

This is my personal opinion, looking from the EU-market perspective.

If you are still strugging for why we use "nums[p], nums[r] = pivot, nums[p]"  or "nums[p], nums[r] = nums[r], nums[p]" rather than "nums[p], pivot = pivot, nums[p]", here is the explaination: 

In Python, multiple assignments happen simultaneously, and both the left-hand side and right-hand side assignments occur at the same time. So when you write nums[p], pivot = pivot, nums[p], the execution order goes as follows:

1. ãnums[p] = pivotãnums[p] is set to the value of pivot.
2. ãpivot = nums[p]ãpivot is set to the value of nums[p]. But at this moment, the value of nums[p] has already been modified to the new pivot value.

As a result, you haven't actually swapped the values of pivot and nums[p]; you've simply set them both to the same new value.

CommentText:
As someone who has been watching your videos ever since you first started your YouTube channel, it is so heartbreaking to hear about you loosing the home you worked so hard for. ð¢ Even more heartbreaking to see you so devastated at the end of this video. 

As a shy kid in the Northern USA, your videos gave me comfort when I had very few friends. I remember coming home after high school and watching you make terrariums in the early TikTok days. This is what fueled me to make my first terrarium (which is still going strong). I remember going to follow your new YouTube channel and watching you move to a new apartment with roommates. I remember when you first soft launched Chris on the channel (which it took me a while to realize was your boyfriend ð) and seeing you soon add Theo to your little family. I remember you making friends with JiaHao and hosting your first plant market. I remember when you made your Staghorn wall and purchased the giant dracaena (which barely fit in your old apartment ð). I remember your plant tours, your relaxing plant care days (which always became bigger projects than anticipated), and your apartment makeovers. I remember when your roommates moved out and you had to restyle your apartment with new furniture. I remember your balcony garden and when you first started the bench pond (which Theo liked to lay next to in the sun and watch the fish). I remember when you and Chris decided to move from this tiny apartment into your quaint, fixer upper cottage, which sadly later burned down. I remember you moving into your new, magical home next door and curating each room to your style, even if it took a few attempts to get the paint color or furniture pairing just right. I remember when you first got Winnie and your travel vlogs to Korea and Japan. I remember the relaxed plant repot videos from your picnic table and when you first got into outdoor gardening. And I remember how satisfying and fulfilling it was to watch you slowly piece together your dream home.

I remember all of these fond memories that created this great life that you had. Although we are separated by a screen, sharing some of these key moments with you made me feel like you were my close friend. That is why it broke my heart the most to hear that your home was gone. Your home wasnât just a place, but rather a symbol of how far you have come. 

With all that to say, although your home is gone, I am so glad that you, Chris, Theo, and Winnie are okay. Even if it takes you a while to start posting short updates again, I will patiently wait. Because you are like a friend. This community that you have built has saved so many of us on our darkest days, so the least I can do is wait. 

Above all else, I want you to remember that this community is wherever Benji is. Weather that be an apartment, a home, abroad, or on a friend/family members couch homeless from the fires, we are here to support you. I wish you and Chris the best as you make your next steps.

CommentText: Your explanation of Dijkstra's algorithm was incorrect. It doesn't explore every possible path. Instead, it identifies the optimal path to a vertex and leverages this to locate the best routes to its neighbors. Since updates happen only once per vertex and each update utilizes one edge (as an edge connects two vertices, it participates in a maximum of two update attempts), the complexity is O(|E| * upd). As a priority queue is used for the updates, upd has a complexity of O(log(|V|)). Thus, the overall complexity becomes O(|E| * log(|V|)), which is quite efficient, and a typical PC should handle graphs with up to 100000 edges and vertices within one second.

CommentText:
React Navite apps launch a local web server that plays the javascript code. Access to api is using a service.
Native Script uses a Java Virtual machine that also plays the compiled code for android or ios, the access to api is made directly by the virtual machine.
Flutter runs an internal engine that executes c/c++ libraries directly to ARM. Access to api is directly done by the engine.
So what we need to answer is which is faster?

VideoTitle: Leetcode 128 - LONGEST CONSECUTIVE SEQUENCE
CommentText:
Nice Solution. Explanation of the linear time if its not clear right away. 
Though the solution may look like quadratic due to the while loop inside the for loop, the while loop only gets executed at the start of a sequence when (n-1) is not found in the set. Worst case for a sorted array, the first pass will run the while loop (n-1) times, but all other run it will not get executed at all. so the while loop will only run a total of n times for the entire length of the solution. 
so the complexity is O(n+n) which is O(n)..

CommentText:
The 'this' keyword inside a function refers to the object that the function is a property of or the object that the function is called on. However, the behavior of the this keyword inside an arrow function is different from regular functions.
In an arrow function, the this keyword is lexically scoped, meaning it takes on the value of the this keyword in the surrounding code. The this keyword in an arrow function does not get rebound when the function is invoked, unlike regular functions. It keeps the same value as the this keyword in the surrounding code.

VideoTitle: HTTP crash course | http Methods | http headers
CommentText: HTTP, or Hypertext Transfer Protocol, serves as the cornerstone for data communication on the World Wide Web. It dictates the formatting and transmission of messages, along with how web servers and browsers should respond to various commands. ### Overview of HTTP 1. **Client-Server Model**: - HTTP operates on a client-server architecture. The client, typically a web browser, initiates requests, while the server, which hosts the website, answers those requests. 2. **Stateless Protocol**: - HTTP is stateless, implying that each client request to the server is independent, and the server retains no memory of prior interactions. ### HTTP Request An HTTP request is initiated by a client toward a server, comprising these elements: 1. **Request Line**: - This includes the HTTP method, the resource URL, and the HTTP version. - Example: `GET /index.html HTTP/1.1` 2. **HTTP Methods**: - **GET**: Used to retrieve data from the server. - **POST**: Sends data for processing to a specified resource. - **PUT**: Updates a resource on the server. - **DELETE**: Removes a resource from the server. - **HEAD**: Similar to GET, but only retrieves HTTP headers without the document body. - **OPTIONS**: Describes the communication options available for the target resource. - **PATCH**: Applies partial modifications to a resource. 3. **Headers**: - These provide extra details about the request or response. Common headers include: - `Host`: Specifies the domain name of the server. - `User-Agent`: Offers details regarding the client software. - `Accept`: Details the media types understandable by the client. - `Content-Type`: Specifies the media type of the resource being sent. - `Authorization`: Contains credentials to authenticate a user-agent with a server. 4. **Body** (Optional): - Used in methods like POST and PUT for sending data to the server. The body may contain various data formats, such as form data or JSON. ### HTTP Response An HTTP response is dispatched by a server to a client, consisting of the following components: 1. **Status Line**: - Includes the HTTP version, a status code, and a status message. - Example: `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` 2. **Status Codes**: - These indicate the result of the request. - `1xx`: Informational â Request received, continuing the process. - `2xx`: Success â The action was received, understood, and accepted without issue. - `3xx`: Redirection â Further action is necessary to finalize the request. - `4xx`: Client Error â The request contains incorrect syntax or cannot be completed. - `5xx`: Server Error â The server failed to fulfill a valid request. 3. **Headers**: - Offer additional information about the response. Common headers include: - `Content-Type`: Indicates the media type of the response. - `Content-Length`: Indicates the size of the response body. - `Set-Cookie`: Used to send cookies from the server to the client. 4. **Body** (Optional): - This contains the data requested by the client and can be in formats like HTML, JSON, or an image. ### HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3 1. **HTTP/1.1**: - Introduced persistent connections (keep-alive). - Supports multiple requests/responses over a single TCP connection. 2. **HTTP/2**: - Introduces binary framing layer, multiplexing, and header compression. - Enables multiple requests/responses to be in progress simultaneously over a single connection. 3. **HTTP/3**: - Uses QUIC instead of TCP. - Aims to decrease latency and improve performance, particularly in mobile and unstable network environments. ### Security: HTTPS - **HTTPS**: A secure iteration of HTTP that utilizes SSL/TLS to encrypt communication between the client and server. - **SSL/TLS**: Ensures confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. - **Certificates**: Employed to establish secure connections and issued by Certificate Authorities (CAs). ### Common Use Cases 1. **Web Browsing**: - Browsers utilize HTTP to retrieve web pages and resources. 2. **APIs**: - RESTful APIs leverage HTTP methods to execute CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete). 3. **Data Transfer**: - This includes activities like uploading files and submitting form data. Comprehending HTTP is vital for web development, enabling developers to build and troubleshoot web applications, secure communication, and optimize performance.

CommentText: Regarding audio fidelity, I concur with your point about Spotify; however, the royalty issue for artists feels rather trivial, as none of the other streaming platforms provide fair compensation either. How does the monthly cost of Qobuz compare to Spotify Premium? And what about Tidal's monthly price versus Spotify? You keep mentioning Roon, but it's essentially just an organizer since you still need other streaming services for it to function; you emphasize it quite a bit, but it just seems to be a music manager for stored and streamed music. What is its price compared to Spotify? I am not an Apple fan, I am not in the Apple ecosystem and do not want to pay for another subscription like Apple TV as well as their overpriced phones and still not touch screen overpriced laptops and tablets. And when you last discussed Apple's high quality audio streaming, it required some complex steps to get the desired sound quality, which is far too much hassle. That is the main issue; it is too much work and too costly. There isn't enough CD-quality or better lossless streaming, with a vast library at an affordable price. This is why hi-fi music fans are constantly disappointed and exploited not just by the streaming services but also by the hardware, which is continuously updated to make minimal differences or to cater to individual tonal preferences. However, I agree that Spotify really messed up with its broken promise of high-fidelity premium that really isn't there. You also didn't mention that the audio quality is like a lottery because most tracks are poorly recorded, even in studios, and me and my friends are often underwhelmed by the subpar recording quality. I'm also subscribed to YouTube music premium because of how much I use YouTube already, as well as Tidal. I don't know about Amazon, it doesn't seem worth it as it lacks the interface or the extensive music selection I'm accustomed to with Spotify Premium. I consider myself an audiophile to a point, but it is limited as most of the music I like and enjoy doesn't have the high fidelity sound quality that I want because it wasn't recorded well. I have to lower my high-fidelity expectation and just enjoy the song as it is.

VideoTitle: Database Design Course - Learn how to design and plan a database for beginners
CommentText: Entity: Anything we store data about. Attribute: The specifics we store. E.g.: Entity-Person, Attribute-Name, Age, Gender. Entity Type: The particular person referred to. Attribute Type: The specific column being referenced. Database Design: 1. Conceptual 2. Logical 3. Physical. Progressing from 1 to 3, we transition from a general to a specific design. Data Integrity: 1. Entity Integrity: How to uniquely identify each user/record. 2. Referential Integrity: Integrity in tables with relationships. 3. Domain Integrity: Refers to the integrity of column values. E.g., a PhoneNo column cannot contain alphabets. Designing 1:1 relationships: This can be achieved in 2 ways: 1. Attribute: All data is stored in a single table. For instance, if we have user data and their credit card number, we keep it in one table with only one extra column, and the table remains about the user. 2. Entity: Two tables are maintained. Using the previous example, if we also want to store the date of issue, expiry date, CVV, etc., putting it in one table would make it about both users and cards, so we create two separate tables: one with user info and the card number (or a unique ID for the card), and another with card information. Keys: 3 main points: 1) Unique 2) Never Changing 3) Never NULL. Superkey: Any number of columns needed to ensure each row is unique. Candidate key: The fewest number of columns needed to ensure each row is unique. Multiple columns can potentially make a row unique, such as username or email address. Choose the column that meets the 3 criteria of KEYS; that is your primary key. The others become your candidate key. Natural Key: A primary key column available in the table with real-world value, like a username. Surrogate Key: A primary key column not available in the table and without real-world value. We add this column to the table, like an auto-incremental ID. Foreign Key Constraint: Action: 1) On Update 2) On Delete. Type: 1) Restrict (No Action): An error is thrown. 2) Cascade: The action is reflected in FK columns. 3) Set NULL: Values in the FK column are set to NULL. Compound Key: A key made up of multiple columns, where all columns are keys themselves. Modality: Indicates whether the FK is nullable or not, denoted by nullable(1) and not nullable(0), essentially stating that at least 0 or 1 values are required. ( ) for quick revision. Database Normalization: 1NF: 1) Columns should have atomic (single) values. 2) There should be no duplicates. 2NF: 1) Must be in 1NF. 2) There should be no partial dependency. Point 2: If a primary key isn't composite, it's automatically in 2NF. If composite, and a non-key column in a table depends on partial columns of the composite key (i.e., not dependent on all columns forming the composite key), it's not in 2NF, and we need to create a separate table to remove this. 3NF: 1) Must be in 2NF. 2) There should be no transitive dependency. Indexes: If you have an index on two columns (ln and fn), then in the WHERE clause: 1) Using both ln and fn will hit the index. 2) Using only ln (being on the left) will hit the index. 3) Using only fn (being on the right) will not hit the index. Points 2 & 3 work in MySQL; verification is needed for other Databases.

VideoTitle: This video will change your mind about the AI hype
CommentText: The problem with these LLMs stems from their reliance on bell curve distributions, or probability distributions, to generate answers. They base their outputs on the most frequent information, which is obviously the core of their learning process. This presents three key problems. Firstly, they are not capable of producing truly exceptional answers. Secondly, as more content is generated using these responses, the pool of high-quality content becomes even more diluted. And thirdly, people will inevitably depend on these as a shortcut, leading to a decline in their own ability to create original content. Additionally, because the LLM learns from the increasingly diluted content, points 1 and 2 will be accelerated. Unless there are effective strategies to dramatically overcome this issue, I'm convinced this technology is ultimately flawed.

VideoTitle: 8 Design Patterns EVERY Developer Should Know
CommentText: Honestly, after more than ten years of coding, I've found that over-engineering, including the needless application of patterns and abstractions, is often the worst problem. In most cases, you should just write the simplest code you need. If there's a clear need to simplify, factorize, or generalize (actual needs, not hypothetical ones), then carefully consider introducing a pattern. Document your reasoning, and discuss it with others. But for goodness sake, minimize abstractions and patterns. Object-oriented programming might sound great in theory, but in practice, it makes code so hard to follow. Instead of just jumping to a function's definition (which takes a second), I have to read your factory, understand every possibility (sometimes I even need to use a debugger) to see what the factory does, then possibly how inheritance is being used, and if there's a strategy method that calls other methods, I have to understand that as well. Complexity is always the problem. It wastes resources, creates bugs, and makes the code impossible to understand. Please just keep things simple.

CommentText:
The point Jordan made about gender fluidity starting at 2:52 is a thought I resonate with deeply. In school I did theater, chorus, and took up the elective of cooking once given the opportunity to go to trade school. I was also involved in sports. I loved gym class (contrary to a lot of my friends from other classes/electives) and was on the swim team as well as the ultimate frisbee team. I totally feel the point he is making. I would (and still do) act more feminine while around women, and more masculine around men. I doubt this is an uncommon occurrence, but I never felt like it took away from me as a person or made me a female. I definitely prefer hanging out with women though. I would get called every homophobic slur in the book because I happened to be more flamboyant than most men my age. People STILL assume that I'm gay at age 29 because of my mannerisms and personality, but I've been straight my entire life. I just happen to be a flamboyant, straight, MAN. That comes with all of its own struggles, but it doesn't change who I am. I can't just hop into a new body because I happen to exhibit some feminine traits.

I care far more about people than things. I spend a lot of my time thinking about social interactions and the nuances of first impressions, body language, and facial expressions. This is partly because it greatly benefits my job as a salesman, but also that it just interests me to no end. I am not motivated by money, but about learning more about people in general. A clinical psychologist as skilled as Jordan has such a great degree of understanding of people that he comes off as robotic and almost uncaring sometimes. That couldn't be further from the truth. I would love to meet Jordan someday, even just to have a 1 on 1 discussion about the nuances of interpersonal relationships, body language, tendencies between personality types and the list goes on. I exhibit gender-fluidity, but I have felt like a man my entire life regardless of how feminine I can act. 

I fear sometimes that if I had been born under different circumstances that I would have been subject to gender reassignment surgery. My eldest sister is gay, and given my personality my parents were basically waiting for me to come out of the closet until it was painfully obvious that I was attracted to women. I definitely exhibited feminine traits at school though. I could see a world where someone took advantage of my naivety and convinced me that I am a girl's brain in a guy's body, even though now that I'm an adult that's clearly ridiculous. I'm just a man who happens to be more feminine. It's literally that simple. Men and boys like me will be convinced by very evil people to pump themselves full of hormones and chop their penises off for really terrible reasons. As a child I definitely had thoughts that I wished I was a girl because things seemed so much easier, but that is just a thought that I imagine girls have about being a boy too, especially while going through puberty. Those thoughts that I had boiled down to really simple things like how women were treated around me, and how I was tired of being called a f*g every day. That doesn't make me not a man.

Thank you Jordan, for everything you do. Listening to someone as intelligent as you articulate thoughts that I engage with all the time is just fantastic.

CommentText:
I don't think 7:36:00 is correct:
Memoization-exclusive time complexity doesn't seem to be 2^m+n, given m and n are the nums of elements in two sequences.

first, finding the longest common subsequence by quick sort would be meaningless if one of the lists/sequences is exhausted, regardless of the remainders within the other. That means, and as stated by the code itself, the code will stop getting rid of character/ element when there's no more comparison to take place, so making "all leaves end at 0, 0" unachievable. (They either stuck in a loop like (1, 0) would generate (1, 0) and (0, 0) or could not be proceeded further.)

So, based on the above, it looks like the tree is not a symmetrical binary and hence 2^x could no be induced from the statement "each element would cause two possible choices to be made". But when we tried that -- 2^(m+n) -- with small numbers, it does approximate what was stated and seemed to be true. Let's say [a, b] & [c, d]. but as the quantity of input gets exponentially larger, I'm no longer convinced that is still correct.

When we're given a fixed yet allocable nums of elements (you can see this as you gambling chips), the max num we could potentially get from them from a multiplication is through the minumum difference between the two numbers. (like how 2x2 > 1x3) So, the worst case where iteration would be at maximum, under the circumstance that total num of elements of both sequences are fixed, would be when seq1 and seq2 have the same number. And now what would be the other extreme case? I'm sure you can tell it's when there is only one element in seq1 and the remainder in seq2. The time complexity of that would be:
(2 x N of the longest sequence)+1
and the leaves would just be N+1.

Now let's get back to the "worst of worst" case. I've tried to construct the binary tree up to (4, 4) root and noticed it does resemble a perfect, symmetrical binary tree but with surplus leaves (the number of leaves after you filled out all the gaps left by a zero-sth pairs to make it a perfect binary). And my conclusion was that the time complexity should be of 2 to the power of the height of tree, instead of simply adding m and n. The increment or trend of the surplus leaves is a multiplication of 4 for every one element added to both sequences: I had 4 leaves at (2, 2), 8 at (3, 3), and 12 at (4, 4), so on and forth. And we know that exponent has a greater growing power than multiplication, so eventually the disparity between the number given by m+n and the surplus leaves would be exponentially greater.

From the sum of geometrical series, if we substitute a with 1 and r with 2, we know that the sum of all the nunber of nodes (including leaves) of a h-layer tree would be approximately 2^h. And for a same-number pair root, the height of the tree (excluding root and surplus leaves) is just 2n-2. On a side note, we can now deduce that if we toggle the number on the scale, let say from a fixed total of 10, the number of nodes would lie somewhere between 19 to ~256. Hence, it would be more intuitive (for me, personally) to say that the time complexity of the quick sort that without memoization would be ~ 2^h, for which h is the number of layers excluding root (or counting from 0 if you wanna do so). But, ultimately, it's just the matter of 2^n+2, so I assumed it doesn't affect much. In the end, worst case of memoization (which simply is m*n) would beat 2^(2n-2).

VideoTitle: How not to take things personally? | Frederik Imbo | TEDxMechelen
CommentText:
*Summary: *
Whenever you are talking to someone if the person walks away many people will take that personally and feel hurt. It hurts our ego. The speaker gives two strategies to not take things personally:
	1) It isn't about me: If a speaker is hurt by someone using a smartphone during the presentation, then it might not be about him- the topic might not interest the listener or he might have received an important text or he might be taking notes. When a child is denied something and wails and says 'I hate you', we don't take it personally because we know that it is the child's anger speaking. Look at the other person's intention. Seeing the positive intention of the other person takes lot of effort. But this strategy doesn't always work and that's when
	2) It is about me: It is about your insecurities. When you are being criticized and you are hurt chances are that it is rooted in your childhood. Give yourself empathy. Speak up for yourself. By opening up without blaming them will increase the chances of them accommodating your needs.
	
People may attack you but you must remember that you will always keep your value. Speaker also appeals to the audience to take thing personally for the next few days and then test out these strategies.

You spend 20-40 hours creating what seems to be an amazing solution to that issue, but you get stuck on one part. Then, you look at someone else's solution to a similar problem and immediately realize you still have no clue what's going on, and your solution is like a child's spelling compared to a literary masterpiece. VideoTitle: Working at Google - First Impressions as a Software Engineer
CommentText:
I'm a student working at a mid-sized tech company (~50mill ARR) since my COOP in september and honestly I had pretty much the same experience (tho at a way smaller scale haha the closest thing we have to a personal chef is a keurig machine that brews coffee lol, but we also get free beer).

Especially the lack of docs in internal tools. It's the most frustrating thing to get to a point in debugging where VS just skips over the code where the bad thing happens and you can't just google the problem. Now you gotta look and find the repo and dig into the code spend hours tryna understand wtf is going on only for the senior dev to basically know what's going on and fix it instantly.

IMO the best thing about it is the variety of stuff to do which is what I think differentiates working in software companies vs working in a company with an IT sect. CommentText:
In the mid-2000s I was working for a retail company I will simply refer to as SHC, as an Assistant Store Management. 

As was known by the Store Manager, I didn't work Friday afternoon after about 2 pm or Saturdays due to my Religion. When a new owner took over the company, they added an Operations Manager who in his first week insisted that I not only work on Friday, but changed my closing night to Fridays which also coincided with that same weekend being a weekend that I would have been forced to close. His response to my filing a grievance was that he has the authority to make any scheduling moves that he feels are best for the store and did not have to follow the religious needs even if reported to HR. Human Resources and the Store Manager did block his change for a few weeks, and my normal schedule of opening every Sunday (as such the Christian managers had time for their families, church and the like) but when he tried to make me close on a Saturday, open on Sunday and close that same Sunday, only to have to come in early for a management meeting the next day and then close again, I filled another grievance this time it was one that led to me walking away from the company and talking to my lawyer that same day. They paid out after 6 years of fighting.

In 1999 when I first started with SHC, they had about 5000 physical stores in the United States (not included Auto Centers) when I left in 2006 there were already fewer than 4000 stores left and while the company was claiming record profits, it wasn't going into caring for the stores...probably explains why the company went bankrupt and a 139 year old retail company now is almost finished. Well that and many lawsuits from former employees...

CommentText: It's quite frustrating how the obvious problem of the large block moving into the small block, when the small block is wedged between the large block and the wall, is never addressed. Your x-coordinate calculations don't verify collisions after the velocity update. As a result, the program fails when the large block moves far enough, entering the wall.  The glitches are being hidden by limiting the drawing position and using manual increments of the time steps to prevent it from occurring. The issue won't go away by these methods. The x-coordinate should not be updated until all of the large block's momentum has transferred through the small block to the wall. A while loop should be used instead of a for loop, with calculations repeating until the large block's velocity becomes positive. The timing of the animation is not relevant; by using set amounts of for loop repetitions, it's hoped that the large block doesn't pass through the smaller block. It should instead be calculated as often as needed using a while loop. Using a while loop will cause the program to freeze until the large block's momentum is transferred. However, the counter could be updated every 1000 loops to make it function as a continuous counter, as needed.

CommentText: I've discovered that "fake" fuel lines with various SAE ratings printed on them are extremely common, and have been for many years. I even got some faulty (presumably fake) line from a well-known motorsport shop. It was supposed to be rated for a higher pressure than I needed and for ethanol, but it started to degrade and crack after just a few months, including in a spot that is a known fire hazard on my particular car. I suspect the fuel line you took off was brand new when the conversion was done but was just fake trash, and this is how it looks at a more progressed stage. This experience made me quite cautious about fuel lines, so I swapped it with J30R9 Codan fuel hose which was extremely expensive, and the same type of hose that's used on various brand new production vehicles on the assembly line. It looked, felt, and even smelled different, and it still looks like it's brand new even a few years later. Be careful and be wary when buying fuel lines. Do some research online, check the printing method on the hose, ensure the cross-section looks right, and most importantly, check the condition of the hose after a few weeks and months to make sure it isn't deteriorating quickly. ðð

CommentText:
OK learned a lot, but I think I can contribute.  After two days i can say i can REALLY explain this: (im stupid lol)


********************* EXPLANATION OF sum(i,j): *********************

First we need to realise what sum(i,j) = prefix_array[j] - prefix_array[i-1] means. 
nums =  1 2 3 4 5
prefix= 1 3 6 10 15

prefix[4] = 15, this represents the SUM from index 0 to (including) index 4
prefix[2] = 6, this represents the SUM from index 0 to (including) index 2

lets look at the indexes of prefix array right now: 
0 1 2 -> prefix[2] encompasses all of these indexes
0 1 2 3 4 5 -> prefix[4] encompasses all of these indexes

visualise this as a two lines of specific length. if you subtract 2 lines (think of it as simple vector subtraction)
you are left with 3 4 5. So in the result index 2 is NOT included. But for your result you need to 
include index 2 because of how the problem is defined (we need sum form interval [i, j]). Find the sum  between two indexes! Hence [left - 1]

OK now we have figured out what does the sum means, lets translate it to this problem.

sum(i,j) means what is the subarray sum (of nums) from index "i" to "j"
sum(i,j) = prefix_sum[j] - prefix_sum[i-1] . So basically this gives us the sum of subarray in NUMS (not prefixes!!)! between two indexes!!! In this task we have K that represents the DESIRED sum! so  ********** K = prefix_sum[j] - prefix_sum[i-1]  **********

********************* ORIGINAL TASK: (leetcode 560) *********************
task:  nums =  [1,-1,1,1,1,1] and k = 3. prefix_sum = [1,0,1,2,3,4], "prefix[j] - k  = prefix[i-1]"
Why do we use this form  "prefix[j] - k  = prefix[i-1]", and not the original  "K =  prefix_sum[j] - prefix_sum[i-1] " ?????? (remember, K represents our desired sum).
The point is you can track anything from this equation, because it is an EQUATION. You can store either left or the right side of equation in map. Why do we use map, I will also explain. We will use index "j" to iterate trough arrayy, and using the equation we can figure out what is the i-th index: K =  prefix_sum[j] - prefix_sum[i-1] "  ---> "prefix[j] - k  = prefix[i-1]". 

***** What does prefix[i-1] mean ???? *****
This represents the BEGINNING of a prefix subarray. prefix[j] represents the ENDING of prefix subarray. if prefix_array[j] - prefix_array[i-1] = K, that means in this interval [i, j] exist a subarray in NUMS where the total sum = K. We want that! because we will iterate trough array only once, and when the equation is satisfied that would mean that there exists interval [i,j] that sums to K! "prefix[i-1] = prefix[j] - k  =" equation can bi satisfied mutliple times , that means we iterarte j, subtract K and we IMPLICITLY find the value at index "i - 1". it That index EXISTS IN PREFIX_ARRAY THAT MEANS THIS equation is satisfied ad we add it solution! 


 "prefix[j] - k  = prefix[i-1]" : j=0  -> 1 - 3 = -2 -> that means prefix[i-1] = -2. But that DOES not not exist in prefix array! why do we store it ? This is because is we want to have O(n) runtime, if we searched for every iteration does prefix[i-1] exist in prefix_array, we would have O(n**2). Basically we need only values that exist in prefix_array.   You would have to create a prefix array =  [1,0,1,2,3,4], and each time you get the result for prefix[i-1] you would have to search it if it exist in array. SO for every index j, you need to search index in in array. Hence O(n**2). We want to have O(n) complexity, meaning just traverse array only once! 

 To avoid that we use hash map. key can be prefix[i-1] or prefix[j] - K // remember te equation, it is importat to store some index inside!
we put in map the begining {0:1} because prefix[i-1] case where i= 0. (check the explanation for sum(i,j) above))

Lets go trough the task: 

task:  nums =  [1,-1,1,1,1,1] and k = 3. prefix_sum = [1,0,1,2,3,4], "prefix[j] - k  = prefix[i-1]"

j=0 , 1 - 3 = -2 ,prefix[i-1]= -2 does not exist in prefix array, we put it in map {0:1,-2:1} // we put {0:1} because of the edge case
j=1,  0 - 3 = -3 , -3 does not exist in prefix array, we put it in map {0:1,-2:1,-3:1}
j=2, 1 - 3 = -2, -2 DOES exist in prefix array, we put it in map {0:1,-2:2-3:1}, that means prefix[j]-prefix[i-1] = K, this means that this subbaray totals to K. result += map[-2] = 2

j=3, 2 - 3 = -1, does not exist, we put in map {0:1,-2:1,-3:1,-1:1}
j=4, 3 - 3 = 0, DOES exits in map, we put it in map {0:2,-2:1,-3:1,-1:1} -> result += map[0] = 4
j=5, 4 - 3 = 1, does not exist in map, we put it {0:2,-2:1,-3:1,-1:1, 1:1}.

return result = 4

VideoTitle: Collisions Without a Physics Library! (Coding Challenge 184)
CommentText: Math and physics knowledge is crucial for programmers. I even had to develop an algorithm for a grenade with an impact fuse, and I succeeded. However, programmers often just use a collision callback and detonate the grenade there. But that's a bad way to do it because you need to keep track of the impact forces. The grenade can be hit by solid geometry, but also some external force. I check the changes to the velocity vector. I subtract the current velocity vector from the past, looking at its length. This gives you the impact velocity. If that velocity is above the threshold, then the ball inside the UDZ presses on the spring-loaded plate on which the striker is fixed with sufficient force so that this striker initiates a capsule, which causes a grenade explosion. The code is simple and reliable and simulates the real UDZ of the RGO and RGN grenades pretty well.

In contrast, the virtual DOM tracks the entire DOM as a tree-like structure and updates only the values that have been changed. 4. But some values depend on network calls, so if we update a value, it might be immediately updated via a network call. 5. To avoid this overhead, we can skip the update calls for the immediate value update. 6. The current algorithm used by React is the React Fibre algorithm. 7. The algorithm React uses to differentiate between the web browser's tree and React's tree, formed through create root, is called reconciliation. 8. For the record, I'm a 63-year-old Irish/English/American woman, raised Catholic in NY, and a mother who would take a bullet for her adult son. I have no skin in the game, but I have a brain, and--yeah--a painfully open heart.

def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
    list_len = 0

    node = head
    while node is not None:
        list_len += 1
        node = node.next

    half: list[ListNode] = []

    i = 1
    j = list_len//2 - 1
    node = head
    while node is not None:
        node_next = node.next

        if i <= math.ceil(list_len/2):
            half.append(node)

            if i == math.ceil(list_len/2):
                node.next = None

                if not list_len%2:
                    half.append(None)
        else:
            half[j].next = node
            node.next = half[j+1]
            j -= 1

        i += 1
        node = node_next

VideoTitle: How to Talk Like a Native Speaker | Marc Green | TEDxHeidelberg
CommentText:
SUMMARY
Try to inculcate the following practice to speak like a native speaker
1. PRONOUNCIATION(Focus on minimizing or eliminating your accent ): Read a passage to a native speaker to rate you if you have accent or not then try to imitate the person until your accent is either eliminated or  minimized. For this consistency is the key 
2. PRACTICE COLLOQUIAL SPEECHES: Try as much as possible to interact and pay active listening to native speakers colloquial speeches( lay man definition endeavor to know the way native express themselves in an informal situation) this helps you sound more like a native speaker 
3.CULTURAL TRAITS: You need to know their culture so as to know how to express yourself like a native.

VideoTitle: React Native vs Flutter
CommentText: It's quite interesting that Flutter still doesn't support native YouTube video embedding (though other videos work), and there's no inline webview option for a workaround. Embedding a native UI plugin within a Flutter app isn't possible; you can only communicate with native APIs via channel messages for things like sensor data. The issues for YouTube and map support in Flutter have been open on Jira since 2015. Also, Google heavily promoted Polymer for two years at Google I/O, but it didn't gain popularity because major browsers didn't support their proposed web component spec, like HTML import. Polymer 3.0 now uses standard ES6 APIs, such as lit-html with string literal templates. Flutter seems to have better potential than Polymer because it's self-contained and not reliant on device support. Plus, Flutter is the official UI for Google Fuchsia OS, which might replace Android. However, Flutter widgets are rendered by its rendering engine, not native iOS widgets. So, if Apple releases new iOS components, developers need to wait for Flutter to implement them. Flutter might face competition from PWAs, which are gaining traction on major browsers, as is web assembly. If wasm allows access to native mobile hardware and WebGL, then web apps could feel like 'native' apps.

Yet, these units went in with all alloted vehicle, which further reduced the Dismounted elements of these Motorized Rifle Companies downward to 50 to 60% strength. A lesson that taught time and again with modernized Mechanized Warfare.  In WWII not one Nation had fully Mechaized/Motorized/Armor armies.  They were still 75% or more Foot Infantry which were required to keep up behind the various other forces.  With the heavy Mechaniztion of Russia VDV troops (airborne/air assault) they lack the Dismounted Infantry to be effective.  When 2 -3 soldiers out of 7 man Squad are needed to keep the mounted element going.  That is 6 - 9 troops out of 21 in a platoon manning the mounted element.  The Dismounted elements is more or less at Squad Strength.  At Company level, it means the total Dismounted element isn't much larger than Platoon.  Woefully small force to hold airhead around Drop/Landing Zones much less be effective in achieving their military objectives.  Granted during the Soviet Era the goal was to draw away from the Frontlines troops, but this isn't war with NATO. How I Accidentally Beat League of Legends
CommentText: I've done a fair bit of coaching when I was high diamond/challenger (back then there was only Diamond followed by challenger) and it's nice to see the same stuff still applies: to focus on a gold lead. Now for Junglers it's a bit different and my coaching was for toplane mostly, but pretty much lower elos love to brawl out their brain, someone wins which is often a coinflip, they base and repeat. A kill is worth a lot of gold, but what's worth even more are minions. A full wave is ~100 Gold, meaning 3 of them is equal to a kill, as well as a lot of experience (though you get that just by being around, then again constant fights mean you are not around anymore). And the main value of kills isn't actually the Gold you get out of it, but the downtime the enemy has gold and XP wise. Whenever it clicked that kills are just a tool to make the enemy weaker and not to make yourself stronger, and that minions are the way to make yourself stronger, people started fighting a lot less and instead they just poked. And poked. And poked. While farming. And eventually the enemy who tried to brawl all the time, so they kept walking into the poke expecting a fight they'd win, but backing off prevented that, had to go back to base and a lead was created. Repeat and suddenly you are 1-2 levels up with a 60 CS lead, which is worth ~1000 Gold and way more in stats (especially at breaking points that give ult/lvl up ult). And it's not surprising that this turning point got him on a winstreak right into plat. Even if your skill isn't great, if you just have more stats this can compensate for a lot, and skill will grow over time by doing stuff again and again.

VideoTitle: Vanilla CSS vs Bootstrap vs Tailwind CSS - Which one should you choose?
CommentText:
I think there are additional perspectives to consider, too. Although the utility frameworks do indeed add a lot of character bloat to HTML (making traditional coders think, "Yuck!"), they do provide a different kind of abstraction that some people might lean towards.

Ideas that might gravitate a person or team to using utility CSS might be: You are designing modular systems, developing components using a JavaScript framework, which will certainly use some sort of templating engine. At this point, you may still be adding several classes to style a button, but you do so once for that button component; it may get rendered in the DOM hundreds of times by Vue, React, Angular, whatever, but your template only had you code that once.

I also think that it's a bit of a paradigm shift - a new way of approaching code-oriented design. The front-end community has been going through these shifts for years now, and will continue to do so. Remember when most people react strongly towards CSS in JS?

I'm not actually making a case for utility CSS (I've never used it) but I can understand why some might choose it for certain projects. If you are using some templating engine, take it on! If not, think twice.

VideoTitle: Coding Challenge #98.1: Quadtree - Part 1
CommentText: If he needs to determine the relative positions among n points, he doesn't require n^2 calculations. Only n*(n-1)/2 is needed, which although still significant for large numbers, is considerably less than what he mentions at the beginning of the video. Also, when dividing, the points already within the quadtree remain there instead of being moved within the subdivisions, which is illogical. While it might look visually appealing on the screen, it's a mistake for practical application. He's also attempting to add the point to every subdivision instead of checking which subdivision it should be added to. He includes a simple check to verify if a previous call added it, but thatâs it. If weâre unlucky, we might have to check all four subdivisions. This also raises a question: What if points could be removed from the undivided rectangle, resulting in a capacity lower than it should be? The next point would then have to go there, right? However, that point might have already been added to a leaf previously. I didnât see any solution addressing this. The concept of the quadtree is excellent, but the implementation shown in the video is rather poor and appears improvised.

VideoTitle: Full Node.js Deployment - NGINX, SSL With Lets Encrypt
CommentText:
For a large scale app on AWS here is what i do:
1. All static js/css/img go to a s3 bucket. 
2. My nodejs app goes to ec2 with pm2 for clustering. 
3. An application load balancer is in front of ec2. 
4. All of this is behind cloudfront. My dns points to cloudfront. Cloudfront looks at url and decides if req must go to s3 or elb. All s3 requests are cached by cloudfront. No caching for elb requests
5. I use amazon certificate mgr for free ssl certificate that terminates at cloudfront
This is the most scalable deployment arch that i could do on aws. No nginx to manage. All pieces except your node js code is managed by aws.
I hope folks looking at aws get some ideas from this

CommentText:
*I do speak 5 languages.*
And I couldn't help myself from relating to this video on everything she said...

While learning all of the languages that I do speak today, I had the same fear she's talking about every single time, but eventually I overcame it. 
What I did in order to do so was to find my self a friend that was native on that certain language that I was aiming to learn (I found myself using this tactic more than ever especially with English) and just talk to them about anything that came to my mind at the time.

In the beginning like any other beginning it was always difficult, but I knew that they wouldn't judge me for trying, so I kept going, until eventually I gained the sufficient confidence and courage to the point that I didn't even cared anymore if I committed any mistakes or not.
And from that point on, there is only one way to go, and that's improvement!
Turns out I already had the vocabulary and the knowledge but I was lacking the confidence.

I made a major improvement in these last few months and the video on my channel is a prove of that, in case any of whom might read this comment want to check how bad my English used to be and compare it to this comment which took me like 3 minutes to write.

CommentText: I disagree with the idea of 'separate helper functions' as a general practice. Module-specific helper functions should ideally reside within that module. Functions used across multiple parts likely point to a missing module or task abstraction. These suggestions complicate writing clean code. Similarly, 'unrelated things together' is another way to produce disorder. Also, the one file = one class approach sounds appealing at first but pushes for OOP patterns which is itself problematic.  While not certain what is the best approach, my personal rule is to break things up into modules and files to give single concept to consumers. It is almost the same, but, class is a bad concept approximation. You are more likely to fall into OOP trap if you force concepts into class-shaped boxes.

When I was in my early teens I had a large file saved on my computer of emaciated models who I wanted to emulate. No surprise, I developed an eating disordered that spanned into my young adult life and drastically effected my development and menstrual cycle. Seeing a wide range of bodies accepted and placed on the same pedestal would have had a great positive impact on me, as opposed to seeing images of girls who were only capable of maintaining that weight through starvation. I developed body dysmorphia and an inability to cope with eating or even being at a BMI that was healthy for me. I only felt comfortable to be below that BMI. I have a much healthier relationship with food now, largely because I do not go on Instagram, watch porn, pr expose myself to overly edited images of unhealthy people. Thin is not the epitome of healthy and show casing it does not encourage health anymore than showcasing a lack of health on the opposite end of the spectrum. I think showing a variety is more beneficial. I only wish that they would have not retouched her blemishes (and wish they would not for thin models as well), because that is what creates a lack of health and mental well being imo.

VideoTitle: Stop Wasting Your Time and Money at Universities!
CommentText:
I think there is a stark distinction between computer science and programming, which is a subset of computer science. A true computer scientist isn't just a programmer, but a logician and a mathematician (hell - the first computer scientist lived before the first electronic computer was invented; there are many many CS courses in universities that doesn't even involve writing code, but instead teaches theories that extend into computers). Indeed, complex mathematics and multivariate calculus won't be needed for the majority of programming jobs, but being able to excel at these subjects (even theoretical computer science with its focus on proving things) proves that one is able to think logically (rigorously), which is crucial for programming and, more importantly, for making rational decisions in the real world.

Learning how to use SQL (like I did with your SQL course) is very good. But after learning the SQL language, I think it will make me a better programmer by learning the theories behind how databases work, including but not limited to relational algebra and calculus. For another instance, learning about logical equivalences in a discrete mathematics class has given me the opportunity to think about what I write in the "if" statements in my code so as to reduce confusion in reading my code.

I also have to disagree with the statement that "colleges are scams." The task of undergraduate studies is not to teach you one certain skill, but to make you a better person. After all, being a decent person goes above being able to, for example, write programs. Natural science courses merely uses natural sciences to inspire a sense of curiosity to understand how things work. Social science courses (like history) allow us to see things from multiple perspectives which is super important in developing a mentally healthy person. I have to admit that some universities do these jobs poorly, but from my experience, these courses taught me more of how to be a well-rounded person than of how to use a telescope to observe stars, for example.

Another thing that online courses (not administered by universities or colleges) cannot complete with those hosted by the universities is the unique opportunity to interact with others. Alone, you won't get the experience of attending student organizations of the subjects of your interest. I am not saying that it's impossible, but universities provide a very good platform, already, to aid you in the process.

I believe that an undergraduate college education is a failure if it taught students only how to excel at one subject and ignore everything else. After all, you can get very good at programming just by going online and exploring (like watching Mosh's videos which are great). Meanwhile, if you want to really delve into your major, graduate school is the choice, where you don't have to take any courses that do not interest you.

Algorithm:

Pitfall:
- when shrinking the window, you have to remove the character from your Set data structure as well

CommentText:
Wow. Modern theater cleaning is vastly different than the old days.

Back in the 1980s (I'm 60-I don't feel 60, though!) ð, I cleaned movie theaters, especially the world famous Chicago Theater ( remember the iconic marquee?), we'd first grab a large garbage bag, go from seat to seat, picking up the large popcorn buckets and soda cups. Some still had popcorn and pop in them, so you had to be careful! ð

Anyway, after we "picked the aisles", we'd strap electric blowers on our backs and blew the popcorn under the seats all the way to the front of the theater, sweeping it up when finished.

Then, we'd mop up the syrupy soda, candy, butter and goo off of the floor between the seats, 

Finally, we'd vacuum the carpet between the aisles, the "runners".

That would take most of the night...

The Chicago Theater is big, with over 3,500 seats. The big balcony was rarely open, except on Easter Sunday and big blockbuster films.

Now, on rare occasions when the main floor would be closed due to extermination of bugs and vermin, the balcony would be open.

No blowers could be used, like in the video. The blowers, which were meant to blow the popcorn under the seats, would blow popcorn, salt and dust all over the seats in the balcony, which makes things worse. ð®

So, we'd have to clean the balcony like you see in the video. The floor wasn't as nice, and there was a lot of carpet between the aisles, so no vacuum could be used, either.

I HATED working in the balcony!!!

Anyway, gift cards weren't used back then, but I did tell the rest of the guys that I was going to find $100 one day...

Guess what? One day I actually found a $100 bill! What a day! I bought lunch for the guys, so everybody won ð

I always wondered how stadiums and arenas were cleaned, so they probably did the same thing. This theater in the video has what's called 'stadium seating'. 

I was only 18-19 back then...ð

COLLATZ PROBLEM:
Take any positive number N. If the number is odd, multiply by 3 then add 1. If the number is even, remove all factors of 2, or divide by 2^a, where a is the count of all 2 factors of N. Continue. Do you always end up with the loop 1 2 4 1?
EMPIRICAL PROOF TO THE COLLATZ PROBLEM: 

YES. It will never grow up continually.

3N+1, between 2^(c-1) and 2^c, with a range R, 1/2 of which it will fall at least N/2. 1/3 of which it will fall at least N/3, 1/4 of which it will fall at least N/4, and so on. On the average, it will fall on a number given by the formula
(let us ignore duplications or multiple occurrences)

Ave fall N = 1/2xN/2 + 1/3xN/3 + 1/4xN/4 + â¦+ 1/RxN/N (kinda) /
1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + â¦ + 1/R

take that to infinity we have two sums to sequencies to consider:

Sum of sequence 1/sqr(N) which is equal to sqr(PI)/6 = 1.64493
and Sum of sequence 1/N which is divergent, about ln(R) + d, where d > 0 is the factor of divergence.

So the average fall N = 1.64493/ln(R) at most, R taken to infinity. What this means is that all values of initial N, the problem applied goes to 1-4-2-1 loop in the long run. There simply is no value of N that will give a different loop somewhere else. And neither will it keep on increasing, as the force pulling it to value 1 also becomes much bigger and bigger, or it becomes more and more a certainty of 1. Remember some of them have only all factors of 2, and the solution goes straight to 1.

VideoTitle: Families, firefighters in shock as California wildfires continue | 60 Minutes
CommentText: This is not the time for political debates. These folks are hurting. They are in shock. They need compassion and encouragement. They need the basics to survive. Some need medical care. Many might say, "Why did this happen to us?" We live in a physical world with physical rules. The conditions were there for it happen. The fireman even said even if there was water there stored up, it still would not have been enough. Even if the department wasn't cut back on, there still wasn't enough fire trucks & probably safe to say also not enough trained manpower. The winds went where they may. So please don't say they must've deserved it.  Having such thoughts of judgement is cruel and evil.  So, does that mean you deserve to lose what you've built with your families as well? These are some of the positives to come out of this... a greater capacity for compassion and cooperation, not just for those who have lost loved ones, their homes, places of employment, etc. but also for the existing homeless population, and yes even immigrants. Hold the debate. Some will come to the realization that they have held some things in higher esteem than our creator who truly provides. Yes, the creator provides. He leads you to find places of employment or gives you opportunities to learn skills, etc. It's the person who might turn it away because they believe they are more than what is offered. So another positive is that some folks will become more humble. I pray that all those affected by these fires do what they can to protect their hearts from becoming cold. Instead, look for the positives and open your hearts up to one another. Maybe something as simple as two kind words can support someone who is feeling really down. And remember to ALWAYS trust the Lord... you've got to learn how he works and when you become aware, be prepared to be in awe as your heart will swell with such thankfulness, you can't help but to extend it out toward others. Be the blessing. You will get through this. Things will be different, but wherever you go after this, I promise one day you will look back and see how this experience played a part in growing and prospering you (or your children)... even if you don't see the fruits for some years. I don't know what God's plan for you is, but he sure does. Trust, take a breath at a time, a step at a time. If you keep doing that, you will find yourself somewhere else in 6 months, a year, 5 years. Allow yourself to go through your emotions and then release it. Your life is not meant to stay stationary in one moment in time.
