VideoTitle: SQL vs NoSQL or MySQL vs MongoDB
CommentText: At my workplace, we utilize an SQL database, specifically PostgreSQL. Our "rules" for the schema require all tables to have a primary key as a sequence named either seq or id. If the table's primary key isn't referenced in another table, we name it seq; otherwise, if another table references it, it's named id, so a user table would have a column called id. Then, in the table referencing it, there would be a sequence and a column named user_id. All of our many-to-many tables are named tablename_xref (xref for cross-reference), making the database structure very intuitive. We also include control columns on every table, prefixed with ctl, such as insert user, insert time, update user, and update time. The times are stored as dttm (time with timezone), and any time a user inserts or updates data, it's reflected in the control columns.

VideoTitle: Maximum Product Subarray - Dynamic Programming - Leetcode 152
CommentText: As you iterate through the array, you must evaluate the maximum and minimum product at each position, along with the value at the index itself. If the index value represents the most negative or positive value, discard previous values from consideration in your subarray result. For example, with [2, -5, -2, -4, 3]: At index 0: min: 2 = [2], max: 2 = [2] (only choice is 2 initially). At index 1: min: -10 = [2,-5], max: -5 = [-5] (max is reset), choices: ([2, -5], [-5]). At index 2: min: -2 = [-2] (min reset), max: 20 = [2,-5,-2], choices: ([2,-5,-2], [-5,-2], [-2]). At index 3: min: -80 = [2,-5,-2,-4], max: 8 = [-2,-4], choices: ([2,-5,-2,-4], [-2,-4], [-4]). At index 4: min: -240 = [-2,-5,-2,-4,3], max: 24 = [-2,-4,3], choices: ([2,-5,-2,-4,3], [-2,-4,3], [3]). The result is 24 = [-2,-4,3].

CommentText:
Some words from a Finn:

I appreciate the reporting effort but there are some stuff that irritated me. For one there is the claim about cultural ties. There are of course some stuff that Finns and Russians share culture-wise but Finns are not a Slavic nation. We have much more similarities with for example Sweden, which is almost like a mirror image of Finland, except for different language. Also Estonia.

On top of that, it was kinda funny how the reporter goes to the border and says that "here you can really feel the close proximity of Russia"

Duh, if you go to a border anywhere, you are in the close proximity of the neighbouring country ð

Lastly, about NATO. I personally feel that joining the organization right now probably would not be the best solution. We should, primarily, further boost our own defence capabilities which already are quite okay for a country this small. On top of that, we would need a deeper defence commitment with Sweden that is also boosting its military. Then, in the future, if the time is right, perhaps join NATO at the same time with Sweden so that the risk of escalation with Russia would be as low as possible. Currently the risks could be a bit too high.

It's not easy to live in a tiny country next to Russia.. so these things must be treated with extreme care. Fortunately we are in the EU and are also good friends with Britain & the US. It means a lot to us. More than you'd think.

CommentText: After watching this and some research, I think it's a mistake to rely solely on 'let'. Since 'var' is function-scoped and 'let' is block-scoped, it's best to use both. For instance, within nested loops, you might need both loop indices, and 'let' will not provide the external values. You may also need results from outside the loops. C# doesn't have these issues. So using 'let' in every situation may be a recipe for bugs, more so than using 'var', which aligns with most languages. 'let' should be used when you know you won't need the variable outside of that block. By the way, great tutorial! JS is pretty interesting. Consider global and function-scoped variables.

That is why thereâs so much great music, movies, photos and all different art forms from the past.

One thing I love about older records is the fact that recording artists were just better at being musicians because it was imperative at that time. Writing songs took longer, rehearsals were as important as recording and performing because they knew that they had to nail it at the sessions. It also allowed for music to flow organically specially when songs were recorded with all musicians altogether instead by separate tracks/instrument sessions.

Thanks for bringing this topic up.

VideoTitle: The first 20 hours -- how to learn anything | Josh Kaufman | TEDxCSU
CommentText: I've been using a variation of this technique for 30 years to teach newbies programming. I call it the building block approach. Essentially teach a small aspect of the programming language at a time, get the "student" to use it over and over while being productive for their team. When each building block is mastered move to the next one. In a relative short period of time the student becomes an independent and productive programmer. So, instead of a steep learning curve, there are many short learning curves. Each building block aligns with Kaufman's 20 hours of practice. Thank you Josh!

def levelOrder(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
        q = deque([(root, 0)])
        res = []

        while q:
            node, level = q.popleft()            
            if not node: continue                               
            if level == len(res): res.append([])
            res[level].append(node.val)
            q.append((node.left, level + 1))
            q.append((node.right, level + 1))

        return res

CommentText: The way to calculate the double pendulum is actually not incredibly complex. There's really 2 main things you have to know. 1.) you have to know the physics in order to get a formula for the kinetic and potential energy for each of the masses. 2.) you have to know the Euler-Lagrange equation. you use the formulas for the kinetic and potential energy to get two differential equations, and really the complicated part is the algebra for actually solving for the angular acceleration for theta1 and theta2 because the equations is a little long and both accelerations show up in both equations. The original differential equation is (relatively) simpler and not too complex to see where each part of the equation comes from.

VideoTitle: Backtracking: Permutations - Leetcode 46 - Python
CommentText:
We can use the index of nums array itself and compute the permutations instead of popping the
elements from the beginning and appending it later


def permute(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        
        """ Angle of Attack
        
            - use recursive method
            - base case when one element
            - recursive call to compute permutation except that element
        
        
        """
        
        result = list()
        
        # base case -- least valid input
        if len(nums) == 1:
            return [nums]
        
        
        for idx in range(len(nums)):
            
            # compute the permutation for ith element
            current_nums = nums[:idx] + nums[idx+1:]
            
            # recursive case
            perms = self.permute(current_nums)

            # permutation generated above don't have the 
            # ith element, so append it
            for perm in perms:
                perm.append(nums[idx])
                
            
            # update the overall results with all (multiple) permutations
            result.extend(perms)
            
        #return all permutations
        return result

CommentText: I encountered a problem when importing pyspark (Import Error) in my notebook, even after installing it in the virtual environment. After some digging, I discovered that the notebook was using the default kernel, even though it was in a virtual environment. To fix this, you need to create a new kernel within the virtual environment and select it in the notebook. Steps: 1. Activate the environment using "source bin/activate" inside the environment directory. 2. From inside the environment, use "pip install ipykernel" to install IPyKernel. 3. Generate a fresh kernel by running "ipython kernel install --user --name=projectname". 4. Open jupyter notebook. 5. In the notebook, navigate to Kernel > Change kernel and choose the newly created kernel. I hope this is helpful! :)

CommentText:
I largely agree with the general point but it's also an IQ check, at least of the core PC gamer who is broadly speaking aware of these technologies.

Your point however closer to the end about nvidia hitting somekinda wall is entirely false (same thing happened with 20series since 16/14/12n were just refinements of the same node that was used on 10series which is also why 10series seemed like such a big jump as 900series had also node related.. problems).

It has to do with tsmc's node which is effectively the same as 5n that 40 series was using. Aka why the 5090 is a bigger die and consumes more power. It was physically impossible to get any real gains otherwise without a massive rearchitecturing effort that hasn't happened really in a few generations by nvidia (tensor/rt cores aside).

On the plus side tsmc 2n is looking to be rather noticeable jump and is likely where we'll be in 2.5yrs time so you can expect 60 series go down in both size and power and improve perf by quite a margin. At least on the x02 chip anyway where nvidia are still willing to push performance.

I had a problem where I have n number of players that I needed to shuffle through to build a team, with each having a sum score S. I think 3 being attrackers, 2 defence or something and 6 on wings and a goalkeeper. The goal was to maximize the team skills score given I meed filling the team with the aforementioned, inaccurate arrangement. The issue is, at nCr(30,11), i.e., 30 candidates, the number of needed calculations start to plumber up. I don't say I needed computations but at that point, thinking of pc as an infinite processing power without realizing its limited capabilities, is very... throwing any algorithm hoping any would suffice is an absolute nightmare. At that point  I realized how crucial algorithms are in large data processing, or even extremely small but with exponential growth like this very tiny example that takes seconds, 5 minutes with 38, two hours with just 42!
So it's not the knowledge per se but the understanding of how algorithms scale when using combs is my point.

At last, not all problems require this thinking. If you're doing a game or a gui-like where all it does is take data, arrange it, decrease health and compare it with enemy, straight, simple processing, make the gui and recieve input, then this is totally unnecessary to learn about. I just mentioned it as I found a situation where automation is used in problem solving.

P.S.: I calculated the nCr as if all players are arranged separately, and not the 3 attackers are just 1 permutation. My numbers are way off but you get the point; numbers scale drastically very early on.

VideoTitle: The smallest 'Walkman'?
CommentText:
The smallest "walkman" I had was made by Hitachi but don't know what the model number was, and I've not been able to find anything about it on the internet. It's not the one on the list shown at 6:30 (no 22) as that's a recorder mine was definitely just a player. I found a site called walkmanland and it wasn't in their list of Hitachi models either.   

So if there are any "walkman" experts here this is what I can remember. Bought sometime in the late 1980's. It was rechargeable with a white Ni-Cd battery pack but it could also run on 2xAAA batteries in the same battery compartment. The battery pack did look like it contained 2xAAA batteries inside a case with extra metal contacts on the side at one edge, presumably so it couldn't accidentally recharge ordinary batteries. The back cover had a bump along the long edge near the top of the cassette to make room for batteries. The transport controls were on the top cover at the edge closest to the heads etc and they were all silver coloured (Play, Stop, FF, Rewind) but the auto reverse button was light blue. The top cover also had 3 LEDs in the centre, 1 red LED in the centre to indicate the battery was charging and 2 green LEDs to show the tape direction. The volume control was also silver and was sort of screwed to the back cover rather than sticking out of the plastic sides. It had some very small switches on the top short edge which I think were for Dolby NR, Normal/CrO2&Metal tape selection and possibly something to control the auto reverse mode. I don't remember a tone control unless it had one of those low/high switches. Sound familiar to anyone? It was bought from an independent retailer who was a Hitachi (and JVC) dealer rather than a traditional high street store so it's possible not many were sold. I can't remember if they had this model in stock or if they did it as a special order from a Hitachi catalogue. Thanks.

def reverseList(self, curr):
    if not curr: # this is ONLY for if the original test input is empty, doesn't apply in all other cases
        return None

    oldTail = curr # keep assigning to curr as we recurse down, then the last one will be the one we actually pass all the way back up
    if curr.next:
        oldTail = self.reverseList(curr.next) # stays the same as we recurse back up
        curr.next.next = curr # this is what actually points next back to curr as we recurse back up
    curr.next = None # point to None in case we've recursed back up to the old head (new tail now)

    return oldTail # keep passing all the way up to eventually be the new head

If you have installed many packages, run `pip freeze > requirements.txt` in the project directory while the environment is activated before deleting the environment. CommentText:
Beautiful Explanation. I used the same code for the 154. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II with just one change and it was accepted. 

Since in 154 problem, there are duplicates as well, I added an extra check in case all elements at start, mid and end are the same. In that case, we just decrement the end pointer by 1. Otherwise, the code remains the same.


while start <= end:
            # If the "start" element is smaller than "end"
            if nums[start] < nums[end]: return min(minimum, nums[start])

            mid = start + (end - start) // 2

            # IF this mid value is smaller than previous minimum we found
            # Then update the minimum
            minimum = min(minimum, nums[mid])

            # If start, end and mid are all same e.g. if [3,3,0,3] is the test case
            # Then, we will simply decrement end pointer
            if nums[start] == nums[mid] == nums[end]: end -= 1
            # Otherwise, we check
            # Is this "mid" value part of left sorted subarray or right sorted subarray?
            # If this is part of the left sorted subarray, we will find minimum on right side
            elif nums[mid] >= nums[start]: start = mid + 1
            # Otherwise, we will find the minimum on the left side
            else: end = mid - 1

VideoTitle: Anderson Cooperâs tribute to his friend Anthony Bourdain
CommentText:
After reading and watching the interviews with Tony last week speaking about his last shoot--the Hong Kong episode, things seem clearer to me. He had tried for years to get his idol, the legendary cinematographer Christopher Doyle, to appear in an episode. Not only did he appear, but he got behind the camera and actually photographed the entire episode. To add to the serendipity, his director had an emergency illness 2 days before the shoot. He asked his girlfriend Asia Argento to step in and direct it. She did. And all this happened in Hong Kong--Tony's favorite location. It was truly the pinnacle of his career. Could it EVER get any better...

I know Tony loved his friends and his family, but I think his career (Not the money nor the fame, but the PASSION for what he did) was his life. He lived life hard and passionatly, yet with great sensitivity, and sometimes that passion can drain you over time--especially when you reach a perceived pinnacle that you fear you may never reach again. I think Hong Kong was, in his mind, as good as it could get, and as good as it was ever going to be.

Dear Simon, I wanted to take some time to respond to your recent commentary, as I believe it could benefit from a more nuanced understanding of the topics you discussed, particularly regarding the Second Amendment, militias, and the characterization of events like the BLM protests. While itâs true that the term "militia" can evoke strong reactions depending on the context, for many Americans, especially in rural or suburban areas, the concept of a militia is not a source of fear but rather one of security and local resilience. Historically, militias have been seen as a way for communities to protect themselves in the absence of immediate government intervention. This is a particularly relevant consideration for those in areas where emergency services are stretched thin or where self-reliance is a cultural norm. For many, militias represent a safeguard, a means to ensure their neighborhoods and communities are protected against external threats or even large-scale disasters. CommentText:
This is pretty funny, and illustrates just how awesome capitalism is:

I have a job that would seem like sci-fi if I told 10-year-old me about it back in the 90s. I use a handheld and flat super computer with a built in ultra high definition TV screen that can be manipulated not with buttons and dials, but just by touching the picture OR EVEN SPEAKING TO IT. This magical piece of alien technology can also synchronize with GPS systems, and wirelessly accesses this incredible thing called "the internet" which used to only be for military communications.

It has advanced computer programs called apps, and one of these apps can have my checking account linked to it, track my position, and find people willing to pay me to transport them like a taxi cab would, but using my own car (which is also super sci-fi with it's automatic doors, TWO flat HD TVs that use strange round plastic disks that somehow store video and sound on them which are then read by a laser... a motherf***ing LASER!!!), and not having to report to any boss. The riders also have these sci-fi super computers (which come in all sorts of makes and models, god bless capitalism!), and they can tell it where they wish to go, and my super computer then gets updated with their request, and I can choose to accept or decline the request.

If I accept the quest they give me, the super computer then speaks aloud directions to where I need to go, and displays a map that tracks in real time my position, and their super computer can see in real time my position as well. We can even send text messages that will be spoken out loud by the super computer, or just call each other - WITHOUT disclosing our phone numbers! When I pick them up, the super computer again helps me navigate to their destination, and upon arriving, we can rate one another on a 5 star rating system. This ensures both driver and passenger behave well, as other drivers and passengers can see your overall rating.

Also upon completion, the app on the super computer calculates the costs automatically, and then tells me how much money I made after the app's creators take their cut for providing the app and maintaining the system and booking. The rider can also digitally tip me money, and all of the earnings can be credited to my checking account instantly for a 50 cent fee, or credited for no fee if I wait for the weekly pay cycle.

This super sci-fi, almost magic-like job of mine is an Uber driver. Yeah. Just an Uber driver. 10-year-old me would think my job was like something reserved for space ship captains or black ops soldiers due to how fantastic and unreal it sounds, yet we're so used to smart phones now and the apps they have that we take them for granted. None of it existed when I was a little boy. The state of the art tech for 10-year-old me was Windows 95. CPUs were still measured in MHz, not GHz. The only LCD screens I knew of were on my old TI calculator and the Sega Game Gear. Everything else were CRTs or projection TVs (not to be mistaken with digital projectors, which didn't exist as far as we knew). Hell, my family didn't get our first computer until 1998, and it used dial up internet (back when AOL ruled the world, and "LOL" wasn't a thing yet).

If you didn't live through the 90s, you have NO IDEA WTF I'm talking about. Like disposable cameras. When was the last time you kids heard of Kodak? Probably in the Smithsonian, am I right? Well, Kodak was one of those "too big to fail" corporations that was the king of film for cameras. Then some upity entrepreneurial capitalist went and invented the digital camera, leaving Kodak in the annals of history. Steve Jobs effectively revolutionized the world and nearly killed Motorola when he introduced the first iPhone in I think it was what? 2006? That was about 13 years ago. I lived over 20 years before smart phones were even a thing. It's like goddamn voodoo magic, people. Pure sci-fi turned into reality, all thanks to capitalism encouraging people to take a huge risk in starting a company and seeing if what they have to offer is something people are willing to pay them to obtain. Think of all the jobs that REQUIRE a smart phone. Almost none of them existed prior to 2006, and those that did were terribly inefficient by comparison.

Capitalism gives us things like GPS, air conditioning, TV shows, movies, video games, internet, Amazon, online banking, ride sharing that doesn't suck, cars, air travel, medical innovations like the artificial heart, cough medicine, vaccines, awesome stores like mega shopping centers that can give the poor a means to eat and be clothed well for very little cost, digital chips to help our lost pets get returned to us, harnesses and strollers for our babies, school buses to safely transport our children (someone has to design, build, and maintain them, despite the government owning the vehicles), etc., etc., etc.

In short, capitalism is awesome, and communism/socialism is pure evil.

CommentText:
Best merge tool: kdiff3!
Saved me for a huge merge involving thousands of conflicts over ~100 files, most of which were just different tab/space conventions, but many conflicts were actual conflicts where I had to combine the two versions.
It shows the last common ancestor, the two versions in the branches to be merged, and the version that will be the output; the output version can also be a mix of all the versions, and can include also new modifications.
It has shortcuts to solve the conflicts fast. It allows to realign the code history with anchors in the two branches manually in case the tool didn't do it properly (even though it is not perfect).

Then, by repeatedly inserting elements from the unsorted half into the sorted half, the algorithm eventually produces a fully sorted array. The full steps of this process for an array,Â A, are shown below

- Designate the leftmost element ofÂ *A*Â as the only element of the sorted side. This side is guaranteed to be sorted by default, since it now contains only one element.
- Insert the first element of the unsorted side into the correct place in the sorted side, increasing the number of sorted elements by one.
- Repeat step two until there are no unsorted elements left.

Notice that this method doesnât require us to create a new array to store the sorted values. All we have to do is keep track of how much of the original array is sorted. This makes insertion sort an in-place algorithm.

VideoTitle: SQL vs NoSQL or MySQL vs MongoDB
CommentText: I don't see any issue with normalizing data across several tables when using NoSQL. While it may not be ideal, one could simply retrieve multiple records and combine them in the application code, similar to an SQL join (perhaps slower, but it scales horizontally and can be done in parallel). As a matter of fact, several NoSQL databases now support this. The most significant distinction between SQL and NoSQL is that relational databases must support ACID transactions across multiple tables, which is generally not feasible with non-relational databases (except in limited situations like a transaction within a partition). This is a primary reason why relational databases don't scale horizontally, whereas NoSQL databases do.

VideoTitle: Longest Palindromic Substring - Python - Leetcode 5
CommentText:
Hi there is a small inefficiency in implementing the solution, in the line you have written:
res = s[l:r+1] Slicing is not ofO(1), it takes O(r-l+1) so ultimately your solution will become O(n^3)
however you can do it in O(n^2) by just removing the slicing her is the code using the same approach in O(n^2) : 
***********************************************************
class Solution:
    def longestPalindrome(self, s: str) -> str:
        res = ""
        resLen =0
        for i in range(len(s)):
            #odd len palindrome
            l,r = i,i
            temp = ""
            while l>=0 and r<len(s) and s[l]==s[r]:
                if l != r : 
                    temp = s[l]+temp+s[r]
                else:
                    temp = s[l]
                if(r-l+1 > resLen):
                    resLen = r-l+1
                    res = temp
                l -= 1
                r += 1
            
            #even len palindrome
            l,r = i,i+1
            temp = ""
            while l>=0 and r<len(s) and s[l]==s[r]:
                if l != r : 
                    temp = s[l]+temp+s[r]
                if(r-l+1 > resLen):
                    resLen = r-l+1
                    res = temp
                l -= 1
                r += 1
        return res
*************************************************

VideoTitle: 20 System Design Concepts Explained in 10 Minutes
CommentText: System design concepts explained in the video ð 1. Vertical scaling - involves enhancing a single machine's resources (such as CPU, memory, or storage) to boost its performance or handle heavier workloads. 2. Horizontal scaling - involves adding more servers to a system to divide the workload, thereby improving overall capacity and performance. 3. Load balancer - A load balancer is a network device or software that efficiently distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers or resources to optimize performance and ensure high availability. 4. Content delivery networks - Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) consist of distributed networks of servers strategically located closer to end users. They are designed to efficiently deliver web content by caching and serving it from nearby locations 5. Caching - Caching is the process of temporarily storing frequently accessed data or content in a cache to facilitate quicker retrieval and minimize the need for repeated requests 6. Internet Protocol Address - An IP address is a unique numerical identifier assigned to each device connected to a computer network 7. TCP - TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is a communication protocol that guarantees reliable, connection-oriented transmission of data by segmenting it into smaller packets, numbering them, and reassembling them at the destination. 8. DNS - DNS (Domain Name System) is a decentralized naming system that translates easy-to-remember domain names into IP addresses 9. HTTP - HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is a protocol that governs the communication between web browsers and servers, enabling the retrieval and transfer of web pages and resources over the internet. 10. REST - REST (Representational State Transfer) is an approach to designing web services that uses standard HTTP methods and URLs to facilitate communication between clients and servers. 11. GraphQL - GraphQL serves as a query language for APIs, providing a flexible and efficient means for clients to request and retrieve data from servers. It enables clients to specify their precise data requirements. Using single query it can fetch multiple resources without overfetching as well. 12. gRPC - gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call) is an open-source framework designed to enable efficient communication and interoperation between services by defining interfaces and data contracts using Protocol Buffers and facilitating bi-directional streaming and error handling. 13. web sockets - WebSockets is a communication protocol that establishes full-duplex, real-time, and bidirectional communication between a client and a server over a single, persistent connection. WebSockets find applications in scenarios like chat systems or real-time collaboration tools, where continuous data exchange between clients and servers is essential. 14. SQL - SQL (Structured Query Language) is a programming language designed for managing and manipulating relational databases, enabling users to execute tasks such as querying data, defining database structure, and modifying data records. SQL is used when fast retrieval of data is needed 15. ACID compliance - ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) compliance is a set of properties ensuring reliability and integrity in database transactions, guaranteeing their reliable, consistent, and interference-free execution. 16. NoSQL databases - NoSQL (Not Only SQL) databases represent a category of databases that offer flexible, schema-less data models and horizontal scalability, making them well-suited for managing substantial volumes of unstructured or semi-structured data. 17. Sharding - Sharding is a database management technique involving the horizontal division and distribution of data across multiple servers or nodes, with the aim of enhancing performance, scalability, and load balancing. 18. Replication - Replication involves the creation and maintenance of identical data copies across multiple servers or nodes, offering redundancy, fault tolerance, and enhanced data availability in distributed systems. 19. CAP thoerem - The CAP theorem posits that in a distributed system, it's impossible to simultaneously guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance, necessitating trade-offs among these three properties. 20. Message Queues - Similar to databases, they have durable storage. They can be replicated for redunduncy or sharded for scalability. This can be used in task distribution and workload decoupling.

why there are two tokens(Access, refresh)
- Access token short lived and refresh token long lived.

**Access token** : Till the time you have access token, you can access that features or resources which require authentication.

- suppose your login session expires in 15min, now you have to login again through password.
- so to prevent this problem, you use "refresh token"

**Refresh Token** : saved in DB and also given to user

- user will be validated through access token only, which will be given after login

- but user do not have to enter password every time to have the new access token, if he have the refresh token, same as stored in DB, then we give him a new access token.

CommentText:
The "-sS" flag refers to a SYN scan, which is a type of scanning technique used in network reconnaissance. SYN scan is a common scan type in network security tools such as Nmap.

In a SYN scan, the scanning tool sends TCP SYN packets to the target host's specific ports. The scanning tool waits for the response from the target host. If the port is open, the target host responds with a TCP SYN-ACK packet. However, if the port is closed, the target host responds with a TCP RST packet.

The purpose of the SYN scan is to determine which ports on the target host are open and listening for incoming connections. By analyzing the responses received, an attacker or security professional can identify potential entry points or vulnerabilities in a target system.

It's important to note that performing SYN scans or any type of network scanning without proper authorization is illegal and unethical. Network scanning should only be conducted with proper authorization and for legitimate security testing or troubleshooting purposes.

CommentText: This solution seems to cause repeated DFS paths for each crs within each iteration of numCourses since visitSet is reset each time. In my implementation, I used "visited" to keep track of the path to avoid re-traversal.  I check the length of the value of the selected key/course first to know if we have checked it before. class Solution: def canFinish(self, numCourses: int, prerequisites: List[List[int]]) -> bool: adjList = { i:set() for i in range(numCourses)} visited = set() for a,b in prerequisites: adjList[a].add(b) def dfs(curr): if len(adjList[curr]) == 0: return True if curr in visited: return False visited.add(curr) tmp = adjList[curr].copy() for pre in tmp: if not dfs(pre): return False adjList[curr].remove(pre) return True for i in range(numCourses): if not dfs(i): return False return True

VideoTitle: Coding Challenge #74: Clock with p5.js
CommentText:
I like the end result, but I would modify some things about the code:
- I don't think it's such a good idea to redraw the clock on each frame. Perhaps it would be better to store the time in a variable and instead each frame check if the current time is different. If so, redraw the clock and update the time variable.

- map() is nice and everything, but why abuse it? The "mapping" for the clock is quite simple. For instance, let secondAngle = sc/60*360;   instead of let secondAngle = map(sc, 0, 60, 360);   and similar for minutes and hours.

- instead of translating and rotating the whole canvas (which could cause confusion if more drawings are added later on), you could set the start angle for all the arcs at -90 degrees. Even better, use let startAngle = -90;  and call arc() using startAngle+secondsAngle as the end angle.

- A fancy way to achieve the clock hands without calling the line() function would be to use PIE in the arc() calls.

CommentText:
00:00 Poorly designed PowerPoints are a waste of time and hinder our intelligence as human beings.
02:58 90% of what you say in a presentation is forgotten within 30 seconds.
05:29 Use one message per slide to optimize cognitive and psychological understanding
07:59 Use PowerPoint for what it's supposed to be used for

18:04 The number of objects per slide is the problem in PowerPoint presentations, not the number of slides.







Poorly designed PowerPoints are a waste of time and hinder our intelligence as human beings.
- Why do we continue to create bad PowerPoints?
- The speaker's passion for the brain and presentation skills led them to search for a solution to poorly designed PowerPoints.
- The lack of resources on the topic prompted the speaker to develop their own approach.
- The problem is widespread, even among top universities.

90% of what you say in a presentation is forgotten within 30 seconds.
- This is due to the limited capacity of working memory.
- Working memory is the same for PowerPoint and other activities.

Use one message per slide to optimize cognitive and psychological understanding
- The brain is limited in understanding multiple messages on a single slide
- Speaking while showing text on a slide results in zero retention

Use PowerPoint for what it's supposed to be used for
- Use the documentation field for text and the area above for short, sweet bits of text and an image
- Size matters - use it to your advantage by controlling where the viewer's attention is drawn

Use contrast to control focus
- PowerPoint's built-in contrast functionality can be used to highlight key points in a presentation
- White backgrounds in PowerPoint can be a drawback and should be avoided
- Using contrast helps the audience focus on the presenter, who should be the main visual aid

Limit the number of objects in your PowerPoint slides.
- Having too many objects creates anxiety for the audience.
- The perfect amount of objects depends on how it feels to you.

More than 7 objects on a PowerPoint slide require 500% more energy to understand
- Reducing the number of objects on a slide helps the brain process information more easily
- Perceptive limit of the brain is low, so keep the information on a slide concise

The number of objects per slide is the problem in PowerPoint presentations, not the number of slides.
- The idea of limiting the number of slides in corporate organizations is counterproductive.
- Jamming more content into fewer slides is not effective.
- Cross-examination is a fun way to prove a point and test audience retention.
- Effective PowerPoint presentations should have one message per slide, use contrast and size to steer focus, avoid speaking sentences while showing slides, use a dark background, and have no more than six objects per slide.

CommentText: It's the first sound that I hear when I wake up and it's the last sound I hear when I drift off to sleep... and it follows me around all day.  I can hear people just fine when they face me when they're talking, but if they're some distance away, speaking more quietly or not facing me I can always hear that they are talking, but it often makes it difficult to clearly hear their words.  And, when I'm in a more noisy environment, like a restaurant, it just seems to get louder and complicate conversations.  It's really hard to explain this to the people who are closest to me because they think I'm losing my hearing and keep pushing me to get hearing aids, but they don't understand it's not that I can't hear, it's that I constantly hear something I don't want to hear that makes it harder to hear the things I really want to hear.  This is the first time I've had the opportunity to share comments with people who understand what I've been experiencing for more than forty years.  Thanks for "listening."

VideoTitle: The corpses that changed my life | Caitlin Doughty | TEDxVienna
CommentText: I was traumatized as a kid. My grandmother would make us kiss the corpse in the casket. These were family members that I barely even knew. It was so morbid. When my first sister passed, we decided that my mother wouldn't see her until we "fixed" my sister. I walked into the prep room backwards. I thought that if i turned around and saw my little sister on that table...dead...I would have a heart attack or that my brain would break. It took everything in me to turn around, slowly, and face her corpse. It's seered into my brain until I die. My other sister and I did her hair and makeup. She was beautiful, like a sleeping angel. I will never regret doing this for her even though it completely changed my entire worldview and life from that moment on. When my other sister that helped took her life in 2020, we elected on cremation. Well, I elected on cremation. I handled every aspect of it...but I could not go into that morgue and see another little sister dead. I believe that it would have broken beyond repair. At any given moment, I know that I can take destiny in my own hands and that death is a comforting exit door. That realization, while bizarre to other people, makes sense to me. Death is the ultimate solution that I can employ upon myself at any time and that alone gives me strength. I contemplate it every single day since 9 Sep 2011. I would rather die than live through that again.

CommentText: I'm not sure this qualifies as a sliding window problem. While there are some similarities to a dynamic sliding window, I don't believe they're the same. Feel free to correct me if I'm wrong. Here's how I see it: In this problem, the right pointer always advances, the left pointer moves to the right pointer if right is less than left, the values in between the pointers aren't relevant, and it returns the difference between the right and left pointers. For a Dynamic Sliding Window, the right pointer moves until a condition is met, (and its value impacts a calculation), the left pointer moves if a condition is fulfilled (and its value removed from a calculation), the values between the pointers are used in calculations, and a minimum subarray length is generally returned.

VideoTitle: The power of seduction in our everyday lives | Chen Lizra | TEDxVancouver
CommentText: Here is what I gathered from the talk: So I work in a field where there are many opportunities to move up in my company. Sometimes it requires seniority and how long you've been there, other things require certain levels of experience and education or familiarity and loyalty to the company. The art of seduction in my case, is not trying to sexually arouse my co-workers, bosses, or corporate higher-ups but more so: provide my company with a strong and professional work ethic. If I show them all of the skill sets that I provide from my life experience and from my college education, I open up opportunities to move up. I started at the bottom of my company and I've moved up from working for almost 4 years with the company and showing extreme dedication, loyalty, hard work, experience, and desire to work harder and to move up in the world. I know what I want, I want to move up in the company. My next step is to think - how do I do it? Well maybe I need to improve how I manage my time or find better ways to accomplish tasks to make workflow smoother for the individuals around me including myself and my boss. Perhaps I can take the initiative and take matters into my own hand and solve problems and work on tasks without being asked to. I strive to be punctual every day and I never miss a day of work. With all of these qualities that I carry with me, to them it looks good and it shows that I am willing to work hard to get to where I want to be and if they had to choose me or the person who calls off every week, it's probably going to be me. How you carry yourself, your personality and your way of doing things can be seductive and persuasive over a long period of time. I hope this makes sense to others.

VideoTitle: Diameter of a Binary Tree - Leetcode 543 - Python
CommentText:
I think this problem deserves an update. The way you explained it is pretty complicated. It's way more intuitive to simply count the number of edges.

```
class Solution:
    def diameterOfBinaryTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        if not root: return 0

        diameter = 0

        def dfs(node):
            if not node: return 0
            edges_l = dfs(node.left) if node.left else 0
            edges_r = dfs(node.right) if node.right else 0
            nonlocal diameter
            diameter = max(diameter, edges_l + edges_r)
            edges = 1 + max(edges_l, edges_r)
            return edges

        dfs(root)
        
        return diameter
```

CommentText: "Cancel culture" is an imprecise term. If a group chooses to patronize a different business due to a company's stated position, this could be considered "cancel culture," and most would likely accept it. The issue arises when "cancel culture" becomes synonymous with censorship, denying individuals the freedom to express themselves because some find their views objectionable, or even harassment, such as uncovering personal information and using it to coerce or harass their employers into submission. Social media platforms should be regulated as public utilities, as they function as the modern public square. Additionally, laws should be updated regarding doxxing and the limitation of online mob behavior that could jeopardize others' safety. However, I wholeheartedly agree that "cancel culture" is frequently used as a simplistic dismissal of valid criticism.

VideoTitle: Flutter vs React Native - Will Flutter Kill React Native?
CommentText:
The thing with Flutter is: I really don't trust the Dart programming language to be the next big thing. I mean, it has basically evolved into a language almost exclusively used by the Flutter framework and the fates of both are tightly coupled together. Besides some small projects Dart isn't used anywhere else. Also, to me it doesn't seems to have any significant benefits compared to other popular languages, so why bother learning a new language nobody uses for anything else then mobile app development?

I'm a backend guy who just wanted to create an app, so I tried both. I looked for alternatives for technologies I already knew, but the options are scarce (there's basically Kivy for Python, but bundling Python for Android offers a mediocre DX. Also, there's fyne for Golang, which is pretty nice, but oh my god, it looks super ugly on mobile). I found the React Native approach very appealing. That's funny, because although I didn't know much React before and still think React is too bloated in 99% of the cases when it comes to web dev, I found it to make perfect sense in terms of mobile apps. But who knows, I'm not doing mobile development for a professionally and started just a few days ago, so I might actually change one day, we'll see.

CommentText:
I'd just like to interject for a moment. What you're referring to as Linux, is in fact, GNU/Linux, or as I've recently taken to calling it, GNU plus Linux. Linux is not an operating system unto itself, but rather another free component of a fully functioning GNU system made useful by the GNU corelibs, shell utilities and vital system components comprising a full OS as defined by POSIX.

Many computer users run a modified version of the GNU system every day, without realizing it. Through a peculiar turn of events, the version of GNU which is widely used today is often called "Linux", and many of its users are not aware that it is basically the GNU system, developed by the GNU Project.

There really is a Linux, and these people are using it, but it is just a part of the system they use. Linux is the kernel: the program in the system that allocates the machine's resources to the other programs that you run. The kernel is an essential part of an operating system, but useless by itself; it can only function in the context of a complete operating system. Linux is normally used in combination with the GNU operating system: the whole system is basically GNU with Linux added, or GNU/Linux. All the so-called "Linux" distributions are really distributions of GNU/Linux.

VideoTitle: 5 Design Patterns Every Engineer Should Know
CommentText: Singleton is often considered an anti-pattern and generally shouldn't be used for datastores to avoid global connections. Modern singletons use IoC containers for global lifetime objects. Bridge and adapter are fundamentally different design patterns. What's described as the bridge is actually the adapter, which wraps a third-party interface into your system. The bridge separates abstraction from implementation. The adapter is frequently used, while the bridge is rare. An adapter is used to wrap external components under a class that supports your interfaces, allowing foreign APIs to conform to your system. Multiple implementations don't constitute an adapter, as it's not about polymorphism. The facade pattern emerges naturally through common sense and the strategy pattern is similarly intuitive. Observer patterns are indeed crucial. The core concept revolves around subject/observer interactions where the subject can attach, detach, and notify, while the observer reacts to these changes.

CommentText:
Writing this as someone who swapped to FF14 about 3-ish years ago and has not come back to RS3 or ever plans to.

RS3 (or originally RS2) was my childhood game, as I was poor and didn't have enough money for world of warcraft.
I maxxed in RS3, but not anywhere near completionist cape levels. RS3 completely stopped being fun for me exactly because of the reasons you described.

1. anything I grinded in the game was pointless. Waiting for dailies, treasure hunter keys or buying bonds is atleast 10x more efficient than any activity I could be doing to progress in the game.
2. Completely dead minigames. No, I don't want to join a specific discord to signup for events. I want to play Stealing creations when I want to do it.
3. (not sure if you mentioned this) Insanely different artstyles, quality of overworld, quality of NPC models. Just take a stroll through the dessert, you can find areas that look like minecraft chunkboarders, enemy models from 2009, and super fancy new stuff all next to each other.
4. I do not have the patience to start over again from the start to play ironman, I already put litteral thousands of hours into the game, and don't have the same drive to level my skills than I had when I was a child. The fact that I would need to pay 2 memberships is just the tip of the iceberg.

Those are just the reasons I can tell from the top of my hat, if I bothered reinstalling the game I could probably tell you more.
I'm now happily in FF14, recently got my third Ultimate cleared (UwU, TEA, FRU) and am currently enjoying watching my little brother go through the mainstory. I have also managed to get an IRL friend that I originally got into RS3 to follow me into FF14. She also completely quit RS3 since then.
